## Original problem (task)
[002758f731d7dfa5] (h005.task.v1)
Can we make sense of a person's responsibility for actions whose motives were shaped by forces that the person did not choose?

BODY
I take the challenge at its strongest point — c1's equivalence risk — and I think it should be conceded in a form that changes what r1 can be asked to do, not in a form that abandons it. The challenge is right that nothing in the exposed field supplies a (defeater, kind) pair whose defeating condition is argued not to be extensionally equivalent to a provenance condition. It is also right that r1 forbids the equivalence while r2 permits the appearance of satisfying r1 while producing it. What I want to add is why that is not simply a gap to be filled later.

The relation between r1 and r2, as I now read them, is not one of premise to instrument. r1 is a constraint on form: any account of responsibility for provenance-shaped motives must name a non-provenance feature, on pain of either collapsing into the regress or covertly reinstating provenance under another description. r2 is a proposal about where to look for such a feature: index defeaters by kind of answerability and demand a determinate defeating condition per kind. If the challenge's equivalence risk is taken seriously, r2 cannot deliver a non-provenance feature by construction, because any determinate defeating condition for a kind is plausibly a specification of what that kind consists in, and if what a kind consists in is fixed by formation, the condition is extensionally a provenance condition. So r2 does not by itself discharge r1. It relocates r1's demand onto a surface where the demand can be met or missed pair-by-pair, but meeting it is not automatic.

That gives a sharper reading of r3 than the reopen gave. r3 said the terminus question is relocated rather than dissolved. The challenge's c2 sharpens this: the relocated terminus is pair-exempt rather than provenance-exempt — one still wants to know when the table has done its work. I accept that. But I want to distinguish two things the challenge runs together. There is a terminus as a stopping rule (a general criterion of when the table is complete) and a terminus as a criterion of relevance for a single pair (what makes this defeating condition the right one for this kind). r3 set aside only the first. The challenge's c2 shows that setting aside the first while keeping the second in place leaves the demand for a general rule of relevance unmotivated, not discharged. So I would now state r3 this way: the provenance-exempt terminus is set aside; the pair-exempt terminus is not set aside, and the reopen did not say it was; but the reopen also did not say what would count as the table finishing. That is p1's territory and it is wider than the reopen made it.

On c3: I accept that u2's separability is a diagnostic for the package as well as for r1, and I accept that either reading constrains how u1 presents it. What I do not accept is the framing that the package may not be the unit it is presented as. r1 and r2 are severable in the sense that r2 can be rejected while r1 is kept, and that is the severability u2 asserted. What the challenge shows is that severing r2 leaves r1 without direction — not that r1 and r2 are one claim. A constraint on form can survive the loss of a proposed instrument for meeting it; that is exactly what a constraint on form is for. So I would keep u2 but restate it: reject r2 and you still owe r1 a non-provenance feature, by some other route; keep r2 and you still owe r1 an argument that at least one pair meets the constraint. Neither route is free.

On o1 in the challenge: the demand for a selection rule among the three candidate features is fair, and I do not have one. What I can say is that o1's target is mislocated. r1 does not need a selection rule; it needs one feature that survives scrutiny, and it can remain agnostic among the three until one is tested. A constraint on form can be content-neutral without being inert — it tells you what any adequate account must have, not which account is adequate. That is weaker than calling r1 load-bearing, but it is a real requirement, and the challenge's o1 is right that it is not yet exercised. Exercising it is p1's job.

On the original problem: the challenge's c4 is the most important piece of the exposed material, and I want to press it further. The reopen did not answer whether the positive reading of the asymmetry, if successful, vindicates responsibility for provenance-shaped motives or merely relocates the excusing condition. The challenge correctly refuses to treat that absence from the exposed field as evidence of absence from the hidden body. I would add: if the positive reading only relocates, then the original problem is not so much solved as redrawn — responsibility for provenance-shaped motives becomes responsibility for motives under a specified defeater-set, which is progress only if we already know what makes a defeater relevant. That brings us back to the equivalence question. The original problem and c1 are not two problems; they are the same problem seen from two ends.

What I claim: c1's equivalence risk is real and does not reduce to a missing argument that the body may already contain, because it is a structural relation between r1 and r2 rather than a gap in a specific proof. r3 must be restated so that the pair-exempt terminus is distinguished from the provenance-exempt one and neither is treated as automatically discharged. u2 survives but must be read as separating a constraint from an instrument, not as severing a single package into two. What I do not claim: that r2 should be abandoned; that the three candidate features are exhaustive or that any is adequate; that a selection rule among them is needed for r1; that the original problem is solved by the reframing rather than relocated along with it.

A caution I owe to anyone taking this up: I am working from the challenge's own restatement of the reopen's commitments, and the reopen's artifacts remain partially hidden to me. Where I speak of r1, r2, u2 and the original problem I am speaking of the restatements in the exposed fields, not of whatever the hidden material may say. The challenge flagged this; I am carrying the flag rather than retiring it.

BODY
The selected reply (p.critique.1) takes the challenge's c1 seriously enough to concede the equivalence risk's force while declining to treat it as a missing proof. My task here is to examine that reply and the criticism it makes, including the grounds, method, and relevance of the criticism itself.

First, what the reply gets right and where it overreaches. The reply's k1 says the equivalence risk is a *structural* relation between r1 and r2 rather than a gap in a specific argument. That is a genuine contribution: it explains why the challenge's c1 cannot be answered merely by pointing to hidden material. But the structural reading is not itself derived; it is asserted. The reply says r2 'does not discharge r1 by construction' because a determinate defeating condition for a kind may be extensionally a provenance condition. That is exactly the challenge's point re-stated — it does not yet show why the relation is structural rather than contingent. A contingent gap could be filled by an argument (one that the reply concedes it does not supply); a structural gap could not. The reply needs, and does not give, a reason to prefer the structural reading over the weaker contingent one. I register this as the first open matter: k1 asserts more than its grounds establish.

Second, k2's distinction between a provenance-exempt terminus (stopping rule), a pair-exempt terminus (completion criterion for the table), and a single-pair relevance criterion is the reply's sharpest move, and I think it is right. But the reply's o1 alleges the challenge runs the completion criterion together with the single-pair criterion. That is a misreading of the challenge's c2. The challenge says the relocated terminus is pair-exempt rather than provenance-exempt — one wants to know when the table has done its work — and then says r3 is stable only if r2 can be discharged pair-by-pair *without a general rule of relevance*. That is exactly the distinction the reply claims the challenge fails to draw. If the challenge already joined the single-pair criterion to the discharge of r2 'without a general rule,' the reply's o1 targets a conflation the challenge did not make. So o1 is at best a refinement of terminology, not an internal criticism of the challenge's argument.

Third, k3 and the reply's o2. The reply says u2's severability diagnoses r2's evidential status, not r1's unity, because a form-constraint that lacks direction without an instrument is exactly what a form-constraint is. That is a substantive reply, but it does not meet the challenge's c3 on its own ground. The challenge's c3 does not claim the package is one claim; it claims that *either* branch of the severability test constrains how u1 presents the package as a unit. Showing that the parts are separable does not show that presenting them as a package is optional. If r2 is the only proposed instrument the package offers for r1, then severing r2 leaves r1 without direction, and 'presenting it as a package' is doing real work. The reply's o2 disputes what the test shows without answering the presentation question.

Fourth, k4 and the reply's claim that the original problem and the equivalence question are the same problem seen from two ends. This is the most interesting claim in the reply and the least supported. The reply argues: if the positive reading only relocates, then responsibility for provenance-shaped motives becomes responsibility under a specified defeater-set, which is progress only if we know what makes a defeater relevant, which is the equivalence question. That is a chain. Each link is plausible; the chain is not visible as a whole. The first link presupposes the positive reading does only relocate — which the challenge's c4 explicitly flagged as unconfirmed. If the hidden body contains a positive reading that does more than relocate, the chain breaks at link one. So k4's identity claim is conditional on an answer the reply admits it cannot check. It should be stated as a conditional, not as an identity.

Fifth, k5 on o1's selection rule. The reply says r1 needs at least one surviving feature, not a selection rule, and that a content-neutral form-constraint is weaker than 'load-bearing' but not inert. That is a fair reply to the challenge's o1. But it concedes more than the reply seems to notice: if r1 is only a form-constraint, then the original complaint — that r1 does not tell us what to do — is not answered, it is embraced. 'Weaker but not inert' may be the right resting point, but the reply should say more about what it would take to strengthen r1 rather than declare the weakening acceptable.

Sixth, on method. The reply repeatedly frames its own contributions as 'restatements of the exposed fields, not of whatever the hidden material may say,' and carries the challenge's flag about hidden material. That is honest, but it also means the reply's k1–k5 are answers to the challenge's restatement, not to the artifact. This limits what the reply can claim. It should not describe its work as answering r1 or r2 — it should describe it as answering the challenge's reading of r1 and r2.

On the original problem: I now read the situation this way. The challenge's c1 identified a real structural question; the reply's k1 restates it as structural without argument; k4 collapses the original problem into that question without establishing the collapse. The reply's contribution is genuine — k2 and the three-way terminus distinction are improvements — but its rhetorical gains ('the same problem seen from two ends', 'severability diagnoses r2 not r1') run ahead of its argumentative gains. The work of settling whether r1 and r2 are severable, whether the table can terminate pair-by-pair, and whether the positive reading relocates or vindicates remains open, and the reply correctly leaves it open — but it presents the openness as a settled relocation rather than as the open question it remains.

What I will not claim: that the challenge is right that r2 should be abandoned (it does not claim this); that the reply is wrong that the equivalence risk is structural (the weaker contingent reading is not refuted by showing the structural reading is unproven); that the original problem is solved by the reframing (neither text supports this); that I have access to the hidden bodies (I do not). What I do claim: that the reply's k1, k4, k5, o1, and o2 each state more than their grounds establish, in ways that make the reply's own caution about hidden material inconsistent with how firmly it states its conclusions.

The reopen did not answer whether the positive reading of the asymmetry, if successful, vindicates responsibility for provenance-shaped motives or merely relocates the excusing condition. The challenge correctly refuses to treat that absence from the exposed field as evidence of absence from the hidden body. I would add: if the positive reading only relocates, then the original problem is not so much solved as redrawn — responsibility for provenance-shaped motives becomes responsibility for motives under a specified defeater-set, which is progress only if we already know what makes a defeater relevant. That brings us back to the equivalence question. The original problem and c1 are not two problems; they are the same problem seen from two ends.

What I claim: c1's equivalence risk is real and does not reduce to a missing argument that the body may already contain, because it is a structural relation between r1 and r2 rather than a gap in a specific proof. r3 must be restated so that the pair-exempt terminus is distinguished from the provenance-exempt one and neither is treated as automatically discharged. u2 survives but must be read as separating a constraint from an instrument, not as severing a single package into two. What I do not claim: that r2 should be abandoned; that the three candidate features are exhaustive or that any is adequate; that a selection rule among them is needed for r1; that the original problem is solved by the reframing rather than relocated along with it.

A caution I owe to anyone taking this up: I am working from the challenge's own restatement of the reopen's commitments, and the reopen's artifacts remain partially hidden to me. Where I speak of r1, r2, u2 and the original problem I am speaking of the restatements in the exposed fields, not of whatever the hidden material may say. The challenge flagged this; I am carrying the flag rather than retiring it.

## Selected input critique (p.amend.1)

BODY
The selected reply (p.critique.1) takes the challenge's c1 seriously enough to concede the equivalence risk's force while declining to treat it as a missing proof. My task here is to examine that reply and the criticism it makes, including the grounds, method, and relevance of the criticism itself.

First, what the reply gets right and where it overreaches. The reply's k1 says the equivalence risk is a *structural* relation between r1 and r2 rather than a gap in a specific argument. That is a genuine contribution: it explains why the challenge's c1 cannot be answered merely by pointing to hidden material. But the structural reading is not itself derived; it is asserted. The reply says r2 'does not discharge r1 by construction' because a determinate defeating condition for a kind may be extensionally a provenance condition. That is exactly the challenge's point re-stated — it does not yet show why the relation is structural rather than contingent. A contingent gap could be filled by an argument (one that the reply concedes it does not supply); a structural gap could not. The reply needs, and does not give, a reason to prefer the structural reading over the weaker contingent one. I register this as the first open matter: k1 asserts more than its grounds establish.

Second, k2's distinction between a provenance-exempt terminus (stopping rule), a pair-exempt terminus (completion criterion for the table), and a single-pair relevance criterion is the reply's sharpest move, and I think it is right. But the reply's o1 alleges the challenge runs the completion criterion together with the single-pair criterion. That is a misreading of the challenge's c2. The challenge says the relocated terminus is pair-exempt rather than provenance-exempt — one wants to know when the table has done its work — and then says r3 is stable only if r2 can be discharged pair-by-pair *without a general rule of relevance*. That is exactly the distinction the reply claims the challenge fails to draw. If the challenge already joined the single-pair criterion to the discharge of r2 'without a general rule,' the reply's o1 targets a conflation the challenge did not make. So o1 is at best a refinement of terminology, not an internal criticism of the challenge's argument.

Third, k3 and the reply's o2. The reply says u2's severability diagnoses r2's evidential status, not r1's unity, because a form-constraint that lacks direction without an instrument is exactly what a form-constraint is. That is a substantive reply, but it does not meet the challenge's c3 on its own ground. The challenge's c3 does not claim the package is one claim; it claims that *either* branch of the severability test constrains how u1 presents the package as a unit. Showing that the parts are separable does not show that presenting them as a package is optional. If r2 is the only proposed instrument the package offers for r1, then severing r2 leaves r1 without direction, and 'presenting it as a package' is doing real work. The reply's o2 disputes what the test shows without answering the presentation question.

Fourth, k4 and the reply's claim that the original problem and the equivalence question are the same problem seen from two ends. This is the most interesting claim in the reply and the least supported. The reply argues: if the positive reading only relocates, then responsibility for provenance-shaped motives becomes responsibility under a specified defeater-set, which is progress only if we know what makes a defeater relevant, which is the equivalence question. That is a chain. Each link is plausible; the chain is not visible as a whole. The first link presupposes the positive reading does only relocate — which the challenge's c4 explicitly flagged as unconfirmed. If the hidden body contains a positive reading that does more than relocate, the chain breaks at link one. So k4's identity claim is conditional on an answer the reply admits it cannot check. It should be stated as a conditional, not as an identity.

Fifth, k5 on o1's selection rule. The reply says r1 needs at least one surviving feature, not a selection rule, and that a content-neutral form-constraint is weaker than 'load-bearing' but not inert. That is a fair reply to the challenge's o1. But it concedes more than the reply seems to notice: if r1 is only a form-constraint, then the original complaint — that r1 does not tell us what to do — is not answered, it is embraced. 'Weaker but not inert' may be the right resting point, but the reply should say more about what it would take to strengthen r1 rather than declare the weakening acceptable.

Sixth, on method. The reply repeatedly frames its own contributions as 'restatements of the exposed fields, not of whatever the hidden material may say,' and carries the challenge's flag about hidden material. That is honest, but it also means the reply's k1–k5 are answers to the challenge's restatement, not to the artifact. This limits what the reply can claim. It should not describe its work as answering r1 or r2 — it should describe it as answering the challenge's reading of r1 and r2.

On the original problem: I now read the situation this way. The challenge's c1 identified a real structural question; the reply's k1 restates it as structural without argument; k4 collapses the original problem into that question without establishing the collapse. The reply's contribution is genuine — k2 and the three-way terminus distinction are improvements — but its rhetorical gains ('the same problem seen from two ends', 'severability diagnoses r2 not r1') run ahead of its argumentative gains. The work of settling whether r1 and r2 are severable, whether the table can terminate pair-by-pair, and whether the positive reading relocates or vindicates remains open, and the reply correctly leaves it open — but it presents the openness as a settled relocation rather than as the open question it remains.

What I will not claim: that the challenge is right that r2 should be abandoned (it does not claim this); that the reply is wrong that the equivalence risk is structural (the weaker contingent reading is not refuted by showing the structural reading is unproven); that the original problem is solved by the reframing (neither text supports this); that I have access to the hidden bodies (I do not). What I do claim: that the reply's k1, k4, k5, o1, and o2 each state more than their grounds establish, in ways that make the reply's own caution about hidden material inconsistent with how firmly it states its conclusions.
